title: Dytective online dyslexia screener detects 80.6% of children with dyslexia among 3,644 participants, and two 2026 re-analyses find a demographic confound
summary: Dytective, a gamified online dyslexia test with a random-forest classifier, screened 3,644 children with 79.8% accuracy, and two 2026 papers found a demographic confound in its dataset.
account: Luz Rello (IE University, Madrid), Baeza-Yates, Ali, Bigham and Serra published in PLoS ONE (2 December 2020) a web-based gamified test of 32 linguistic exercises. Its performance measures feed a random-forest classifier with 200 trees. The study enrolled 3,644 participants aged 7–17, 392 with a professional dyslexia diagnosis, recruited through 113 organizations in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Spain and the USA. They were 60 primary and secondary schools, 22 specialized dyslexia centers, 18 non-profits and 3 universities. The authors report that a trivial classifier that labels every child as not having dyslexia would reach 89.2% accuracy on this sample, and they weighted the classes to offset that imbalance. The classifier reached 79.8% accuracy with 80.6% recall and 79.3% precision for the dyslexia class. A tablet validation with 1,395 participants aged 12–17 gave 78.1% recall and 76.2% precision. The authors state that an online Spanish screening tool based on their methods had already been used by more than 200,000 people. They disclose a patent application (US 15/493,060, Rello and Ballesteros). Sudha and Murali (Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, 2 September 2026) trained a different model on the public Dytective dataset. They found that demographic variables contribute more to discrimination than any level of their engineered cognitive features, and a variant without demographics reached an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.7948. The authors call for external validation across language groups before clinical use. In a second independent paper (Frontiers in Digital Health, 23 September 2026), Sudha and Murali re-analyzed the same 3,644-participant dataset. They report that dyslexia prevalence in the dataset differs 4.7-fold by native-language status. Four demographic columns alone reach an AUC of 0.724 against 0.744 for all 192 task metrics. Including them yields a twelve-fold disparity in false-positive rate between language groups.
purpose: Dytective was designed to screen children for dyslexia risk cheaply online. The accuracy figures and the count of online uses concern that purpose.

display.answer: Both 2026 papers by Sudha and Murali use the public dataset from the 2020 study, so all three studies rest on the same data. The 2020 authors recruited participants with dyslexia through dyslexia centers and associations and participants without dyslexia through schools. They disclose a patent application. The 2026 authors have no tie to the Dytective team.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Dytective, a gamified online dyslexia test with a random-forest classifier, screened 3,644 children with 79.8% accuracy, and two 2026 papers found a demographic confound in its dataset.
fields.account: Luz Rello (IE University, Madrid), Baeza-Yates, Ali, Bigham and Serra published in PLoS ONE (2 December 2020) a web-based gamified test of 32 linguistic exercises. Its performance measures feed a random-forest classifier with 200 trees. The study enrolled 3,644 participants aged 7–17, 392 with a professional dyslexia diagnosis, recruited through 113 organizations in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Spain and the USA. They were 60 primary and secondary schools, 22 specialized dyslexia centers, 18 non-profits and 3 universities. The authors report that a trivial classifier that labels every child as not having dyslexia would reach 89.2% accuracy on this sample, and they weighted the classes to offset that imbalance. The classifier reached 79.8% accuracy with 80.6% recall and 79.3% precision for the dyslexia class. A tablet validation with 1,395 participants aged 12–17 gave 78.1% recall and 76.2% precision. The authors state that an online Spanish screening tool based on their methods had already been used by more than 200,000 people. They disclose a patent application (US 15/493,060, Rello and Ballesteros). Sudha and Murali (Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, 2 September 2026) trained a different model on the public Dytective dataset. They found that demographic variables contribute more to discrimination than any level of their engineered cognitive features, and a variant without demographics reached an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.7948. The authors call for external validation across language groups before clinical use. In a second independent paper (Frontiers in Digital Health, 23 September 2026), Sudha and Murali re-analyzed the same 3,644-participant dataset. They report that dyslexia prevalence in the dataset differs 4.7-fold by native-language status. Four demographic columns alone reach an AUC of 0.724 against 0.744 for all 192 task metrics. Including them yields a twelve-fold disparity in false-positive rate between language groups.
